title: KPO/BPO
intro: Each role play has 20 spoken lines or fewer. Lines alternate between the Sri Lankan agent and the overseas customer or client; in role play 9, a supervisor takes over the agent's side for part of the call. Pairs read it once, swap roles, then replay it from the coaching notes only. Every set of coaching notes marks the three focus skills (empathy, timely response, active listening) and ends with a “say this, not that” switch to an international style. That switch is not a correction of “bad” English. The agent never pretends to be in the customer's country. Companies, names, references, amounts and policies are illustrative, so check real client policies before teaching.
models: A recording notice, then an identity check before any account detail (GDPR-style for UK customers, HIPAA for US healthcare)
An honest answer to “Where are you?”: the team is in Sri Lanka, followed by what matters to the customer
Empathy in one line, naming the feeling or the deadline, then straight to action
A paraphrase or numbered summary, ending with “Is that right?”
Every commitment with a time, in the customer's time zone, and a fallback if it slips
Holds with a time limit, a reason and a thank-you
A written follow-up with a reference number, and the customer summarising the plan back

scenarios.title: Wrong size before a wedding
scenarios.setting: Inbound call to the customer team of Thread & Co, a UK online fashion retailer, answered from a contact centre in Colombo. Mid-morning UK time.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Tharushi, 24, customer service agent, one year in the role. Customer: Hannah Price, 33, from Leeds, who needs a dress for a wedding on Saturday.
scenarios.resolution: Hannah gets a size 12 in another colour the next day, a returns label within ten minutes and a refund timeline, and she can repeat the whole plan back.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Name the feeling and the deadline together: “that's frustrating when you've got a date to work to.” Then move straight to action.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Every promise has a time: delivery tomorrow, the label in ten minutes, the refund within five working days, tracking this evening.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Tharushi paraphrases the facts (ordered 12, received 14, needed by Saturday) before checking stock, and lets Hannah summarise at the end.

notes.label: call basics
notes.text: Recording notice first, identity check before any order details, and a hold with a time limit and a thank-you afterwards.

sayThis.say: May I have your name, please?

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: Thank you for calling Thread & Co. This call may be recorded for training and quality purposes. My name is Tharushi. May I have your name, please?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: It's Hannah Price. I'm calling about a dress I ordered.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: Thank you, Hannah. Before I open your order, could you confirm your postcode and the email address on your account?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: LS6 2QT, and it's hannahprice88 at mail dot com.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: Thank you, that matches. How can I help with the dress?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: It came in a size 14 and I ordered a 12. I need it for a wedding on Saturday, and honestly I'm a bit stressed.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: I'm sorry, that's frustrating when you've got a date to work to. So you ordered a size 12, received a 14, and you need the right size before Saturday. Is that right?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: Exactly. Can you just swap it?

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: Let me check the stock. Could I put you on hold for about two minutes while I do that?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: Fine.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: Thank you for holding, Hannah. I'm afraid the size 12 in navy is out of stock, but it's in stock in emerald green in a size 12.

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: Oh no. Hmm. Green could work, actually. But will it arrive in time?

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: If I place the order now, before 2 p.m. UK time, it goes out by next-day delivery and arrives tomorrow, Thursday. I'll cover the delivery charge, because the mistake was ours.

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: That's good. And what about the wrong one?

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: I'll email you a free returns label within the next ten minutes. Once the warehouse receives the size 14, your refund of £68 goes back to your card within five working days.

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: Okay. So, green dress tomorrow, label in ten minutes, refund when they get the old one back.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: That's exactly right. You'll also get a tracking link by email this evening. Is there anything else I can help with?

lines.name: Hannah Price
lines.text: No, that's brilliant. Thank you, Tharushi.

lines.name: Tharushi
lines.text: You're welcome, Hannah. Enjoy the wedding!

scenarios.title: Locked out before a client meeting
scenarios.segment: A password and authenticator lockout for a corporate client's employee
scenarios.setting: Early-morning shift at a Colombo IT service desk that supports a Sydney accounting firm. 9:20 a.m. in Sydney.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Ishan, 27, service desk analyst. Caller: Mia Chen, 29, an accountant at the firm's Parramatta office, phoning from her car.
scenarios.resolution: Mia is back in her account with a new password and her authenticator linked to the new phone before her 10 a.m. meeting, and the ticket stays open until 11 a.m. Sydney time.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: “Let's get you back in before then” shows Ishan heard the deadline. Under time pressure, empathy is speed plus calm.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Small promises count too: a text within a minute, and the ticket open until 11 a.m. in the caller's time zone, not Colombo time.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: An open question (“what happened just before…?”) brings out the real cause, and Ishan splits it into two issues before fixing either.

notes.label: call basics
notes.text: Ishan says the team is in Colombo and verifies identity before he unlocks anything.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: IT Service Desk, this is Ishan. I'm with your firm's support team in Colombo. Who am I speaking with?

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Hi, it's Mia Chen from the Parramatta office. I'm locked out, and I've got a client meeting at ten.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Hi Mia, let's get you back in before then. For security, could you give me your employee ID and your manager's name?

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: It's 40217, and my manager is Raj Patel.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Thanks, Mia, that matches. Can you tell me what happened just before you were locked out?

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: I changed my password on Friday. Then I got a new phone over the weekend, and now the code app doesn't work.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Okay, so there are two things: the new password, and the authenticator app that's still linked to your old phone. Is that right?

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Yes. Sorry, can you hear me? I'm on speaker in the car park.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Yes, I can hear you clearly. Can you hear me okay?

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Yep, all good.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Great. I've unlocked your account and sent a temporary password to your mobile by text. It should arrive within a minute.

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Got it.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Log in with that, and you'll be asked to set a new password. Then you'll see a QR code to link the app on your new phone.

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Okay… password changed. Scanning the code now. It says “account added”.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Perfect. Please approve the test sign-in I'm sending you now.

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Done. I'm in! Outlook's loading.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: Brilliant. I'll keep the ticket open until 11 a.m. Sydney time. If anything doesn't sync by then, reply to the ticket email and it comes straight to me.

lines.name: Mia Chen
lines.text: Thanks, Ishan. You've saved my morning.

lines.name: Ishan
lines.text: My pleasure, Mia. Good luck with the meeting.

scenarios.title: Why has my broadband bill gone up?
scenarios.segment: A bill increase after an introductory deal ends
scenarios.setting: Inbound call to BrightLine, a UK broadband provider, handled by its customer team in Sri Lanka. Early afternoon UK time.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Nadeesha, 26, customer service agent. Customer: Gary Wood, 64, retired, from Bristol.
scenarios.resolution: Gary moves to a £30 contract from his next bill, gets a £13 credit, and has a written confirmation and a reference with a clear “by 6 p.m.” fallback.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Acknowledge the surprise before the explanation. The letter in August is a fact, not a reason to blame the customer.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: “Within the hour” plus a fallback (“if it hasn't arrived by 6 p.m.…”) tells the customer exactly when to worry and what to do.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Nadeesha repeats both prices so Gary knows she has the numbers right before she checks the contract.

notes.label: cross-cultural
notes.text: “Thanks, love” is ordinary friendliness from many older British callers, not flirting. Reply warmly and use his name.

sayThis.say: Could I put you on hold for two minutes?

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Good afternoon, BrightLine customer service. Calls are recorded for quality and training. My name is Nadeesha. Who am I speaking to?

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: Gary Wood. My bill's gone up from £28 to £41, and nobody told me.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: I'm sorry, Mr Wood. A jump like that out of the blue would worry anyone. Could I take your postcode and the last four digits of your account number?

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: BS7 9LP. The account ends 3381.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Thank you. And for security, the first line of your address?

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: 14 Cedar Road.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Thank you, that's all confirmed. So your monthly bill has gone from £28 to £41, and you weren't told why. Is that right?

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: That's right. Are you in Bristol?

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: No, I'm in BrightLine's customer team in Sri Lanka, but I can see everything on your account. Could I put you on hold for two minutes while I check your contract?

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: Go on, then.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Thank you for holding, Mr Wood. Your 18-month introductory price ended on the 1st, so the standard price of £41 started. A letter and an email went out in August.

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: I never read those. Can't I go back to £28?

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Not on the same deal, but I can offer a new 24-month contract at £30 a month, with the same speed. There's no fee to switch.

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: £30. And when does that start?

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: From your next bill on the 1st of December. And as you weren't aware of the change, I can credit back £13, the difference for this month.

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: That's fair. Go on, then.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: Done. You'll get a confirmation email within the hour with the new price and the £13 credit. If it hasn't arrived by 6 p.m. today, call us and quote reference BL-58210.

lines.name: Gary Wood
lines.text: Right. Thanks, love.

lines.name: Nadeesha
lines.text: You're welcome, Mr Wood. Have a good afternoon.

scenarios.title: A $480 bill the insurance should have paid
scenarios.setting: Inbound call to the billing office of Lakeside Family Clinic, Columbus, Ohio, handled by its revenue cycle team in Sri Lanka. 10 a.m. US Eastern time.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Dinuka, 30, patient billing specialist. Customer: Denise Morales, 41, mother and guarantor for her daughter Lily, 12.
scenarios.resolution: The coding error is owned and corrected, the claim is resubmitted within two business days, the account is put on hold, and a dated, time-boxed callback is booked in the patient's time zone.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: When money is tight, reassure before you explain: “I don't want you worrying about a bill that may not be yours.”

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Two kinds of commitment: what you control (resubmit within two business days) and what you don't (the insurer). For the second, promise a check date, not an outcome.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Dinuka restates the date, amount and expectation, then asks one targeted question that finds the cause.

notes.label: call basics
notes.text: In US healthcare, verify the patient's identity and the caller's right to the account before saying anything about the bill (HIPAA). If asked, say honestly where the team is based.

sayThis.say: “I'd like to check one thing” or “I have a question”

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: Lakeside Family Clinic billing office, this is Dinuka. This call is recorded. How may I help you?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: Hi. I got a bill for $480 for my daughter's visit in September, and I thought insurance covered it.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: I can look into that. Before I discuss any account details, I need to verify your identity for privacy reasons. Could I have the patient's full name and date of birth?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: Lily Morales, March 3rd, 2014. I'm her mom, Denise.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: Thank you. And could you confirm the billing address, and that you're the guarantor on the account?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: 1220 Maple Drive, Columbus. Yes, I'm the guarantor.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: Thank you, Ms. Morales, that's verified. So Lily's visit on September 12th was billed at $480, and you expected your insurance to pay it. Is that correct?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: Yes. We have a $40 copay, and I paid that at the desk. Honestly, I can't afford $480 right now.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: I understand, and I don't want you worrying about a bill that may not be yours. I'd like to check one thing: did Lily have anything else done that day, like a test or a vaccine?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: A strep test, that's all.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: That helps. I can see the claim was denied because the strep test was sent with the wrong code. That was our error, not yours.

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: So I don't have to pay it?

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: Not while we fix it. I'll correct the code and resubmit the claim to your insurer within two business days, and I'll put your account on hold so you won't get any more statements.

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: And how long does the insurance take?

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: It can take a few weeks. I'll check the status myself on November 20th and call you that day. Is the number ending 4471 the best one?

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: Yes. Mornings are best. Where are you calling from, by the way? You don't sound local.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: I'm part of the clinic's billing team, based in Sri Lanka. I'll call you between 9 and 11 a.m. Eastern time on the 20th.

lines.name: Denise Morales
lines.text: Okay. Thank you for actually explaining it.

lines.name: Dinuka
lines.text: You're welcome, Ms. Morales. Your reference number is LFC-77031.

scenarios.title: Storm damage: lodging a home claim offshore
scenarios.setting: Inbound call to Coastline Insurance's home claims line, answered by its claims team in Colombo. 8:30 a.m. in Brisbane, after an overnight storm.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Sachini, 29, claims consultant. Customer: Peter Walsh, 55, homeowner in Brisbane, with water coming through a bedroom ceiling.
scenarios.resolution: The claim is lodged on the first call, an emergency roofer will call within two hours, an assessor within two business days, and Peter has a claim number, a direct line and a midday fallback.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Safety before paperwork. Asking about people and power first tells the customer you care about more than the claim form.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: A staged plan with a time on each stage (two hours, two business days, midday Brisbane time) turns a crisis into steps.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Sachini summarises the damage and then asks “Is anything else damaged?”, which brings out the carpet and the plaster.

notes.label: call basics
notes.text: Answer “Are you in Australia?” truthfully and at once, then say what matters to the customer: the same policy and the same rules apply.

sayThis.say: A roofer will call you within two hours
sayThis.not: Your issue will be sorted out soon.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: Good morning, Coastline Insurance claims. Calls are recorded. My name is Sachini. Who am I speaking with?

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: Peter Walsh. A storm ripped tiles off my roof last night, and water's coming through the bedroom ceiling.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: I'm really sorry, Peter, that sounds stressful. First, is everyone safe, and is the electricity off near the leak?

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: We're all safe. I've turned the power off to that room.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: Good thinking. To open the claim, could you confirm your policy number and date of birth?

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: HC-2290415, and the 9th of June 1971. Are you in Australia, by the way?

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: No, I'm in Coastline's claims team in Colombo, Sri Lanka. Your claim is handled under the same policy and the same Australian rules.

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: Right. So what happens now? It's still raining.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: Let me make sure I have it all: tiles off the roof, water through one bedroom ceiling, power off to that room, and it's still raining. Is anything else damaged?

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: The carpet's soaked, and there's a crack in the ceiling plaster.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: Thank you. I'm lodging the claim now, and I'm booking an emergency roofer to put a tarp on today. They'll call you within two hours.

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: Today? That's a relief. What about the cost?

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: We arrange and pay for the emergency make-safe work. Your excess is $500, and it's taken off the final settlement, not paid today.

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: Okay. And the ceiling and the carpet?

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: An assessor will contact you within two business days to book a visit. Please take photos of the damage now and keep any receipts.

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: So, a roofer within two hours, an assessor within two days, and photos from me.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: Exactly right. Your claim number is CL-886102. I'll text it to you now, with my direct line.

lines.name: Peter Walsh
lines.text: Thanks, Sachini. You've been really clear.

lines.name: Sachini
lines.text: You're welcome, Peter. If the roofer hasn't called by midday Brisbane time, ring me straight back.

scenarios.title: A VAT deadline and missing invoices
scenarios.segment: A B2B account manager covers for a colleague, explains a reconciliation gap and protects a VAT deadline
scenarios.setting: Scheduled video call between LedgerBridge, a Colombo bookkeeping firm, and a small-business client in Manchester. 11 a.m. UK time, the week before the VAT return for the September quarter is due on 7 November.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Kavindi, 32, account manager and part-qualified CIMA accountant. Client: Sarah Owens, 45, owner of three cafés.
scenarios.resolution: Sarah knows exactly what is missing, what she must send by Friday noon, what happens if it doesn't arrive, and when she will see and approve the return, so the deadline is safe either way.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: With a business client, empathy sounds like ownership: “That's fair, and I'm sorry we didn't update you.” Don't hide behind the absent colleague.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Give the client a deadline as specific as your own (Friday at noon UK time) and a plan B, so one missed step can't sink the filing.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Kavindi checks her understanding of why the invoices are missing before she suggests a fix, and the fix targets that cause.
Say no well: “I'd rather not”, plus the reason and an alternative, protects the client without lecturing her.

sayThis.say: Could you ask the manager to forward the three invoices by Friday at noon UK time?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: Hi Sarah, it's Kavindi from LedgerBridge in Colombo. Thanks for making time. Is this still a good moment?

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Yes, but I'm worried. My VAT return is due on the 7th, and I haven't heard anything this week.

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: That's fair, and I'm sorry we didn't update you. Nimesha, your usual bookkeeper, is on leave this week, so I'm covering your account personally.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Okay. So where are we?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: The September quarter is reconciled except for one gap: £2,340 in card payments to CleanPro, your cleaning supplier, with no invoices behind them.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: CleanPro emails its invoices to the Didsbury café, not to me.

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: That explains it. So the invoices exist, but they go to the Didsbury manager's inbox. Is that right?

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Yes. Can't you just put the VAT in anyway?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: I'd rather not. Without the invoices, HMRC could refuse that VAT claim. Could you ask the Didsbury manager to forward the three invoices by Friday at noon UK time?

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: I'll message her now. What if she doesn't?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: Then I'll file on time without that £390 of VAT, and we'll claim it in a later return once we have the invoices. Either way, you won't miss the deadline.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Good. Can we stop this happening again?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: Yes. I'd suggest CleanPro sends its invoices to your bookkeeping inbox. I'll draft that email today for you to send.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Perfect. When will I see the return?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: I'll send you the draft return on Monday by 10 a.m. UK time. Once you approve it, I'll file it the same day, well before the 7th.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: Fine. And when is Nimesha back?

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: Next Wednesday. I'll brief her, and I'll stay copied on your emails until the return is filed.

lines.name: Sarah Owens
lines.text: That's reassuring. Thanks, Kavindi.

lines.name: Kavindi
lines.text: Thank you, Sarah. I'll send you a summary of today's call within the hour.

scenarios.title: Three problems, four weeks to Black Friday
scenarios.segment: A multi-issue technical case with a direct American customer
scenarios.channel: Technical support for an e-commerce software platform (US)
scenarios.setting: Inbound support call to ShopStack, an online-store software platform, answered by its support team in Colombo during the US afternoon (a night shift in Sri Lanka).
scenarios.characters: Agent: Ravindu, 28, tier-two technical support. Customer: Jake Turner, 36, owner of an online sneaker store in Austin, Texas.
scenarios.resolution: All three issues are fixed or in hand on one call, in the order that mattered most to the customer, with a next-day check promised in his own time zone.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Link the problem to the customer's real fear (overselling, refunds, a bad review), not just the technical fault.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Say how long each fix takes (“about five minutes”) and make the follow-up specific: an email by 10 a.m. Central time tomorrow.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Number the issues out loud, then ask which matters most. This is the core skill for multi-issue cases.

notes.label: cross-cultural
notes.text: Many American customers are direct (“Do it”, “You've got a mess”). That isn't rude. Match the pace, keep sentences short, and learn idioms such as “ballpark” (rough estimate) and “circle back” (follow up).

sayThis.not: “Is it?” as a reply to show you are listening.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: ShopStack support, this is Ravindu. This call is recorded. What can I help you with today?

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Hey, Ravindu. Look, I've got a mess. Inventory's not syncing, customers are getting two order emails, and my new hire can't log in. Black Friday's in four weeks.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Got it. That's a lot at once, and with Black Friday coming I understand the pressure. Can I confirm your store URL and the account owner's email?

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: kickzaustin.com, and it's jake at kickzaustin dot com.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Thanks, Jake, you're verified. Let me play it back: one, stock levels aren't syncing; two, duplicate order emails; three, a staff login problem. Which is hurting you most right now?

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: The inventory. I sold a pair yesterday that I didn't have. That's a refund and a bad review.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: I see. That's the worst kind of problem for a small store. When did the sync last work, as far as you know?

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Ballpark? Monday. I updated the warehouse app Monday night.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: That's useful. The update reset the connection key, and I can see the sync failed at 11:42 p.m. on Monday. I'll walk you through reconnecting it now. It takes about five minutes.

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Do it.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: In Settings, open Apps, then Warehouse Sync, and click Reconnect. Then approve the request on the warehouse side.

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Okay… it says “Connected. Syncing 1,204 items.” Awesome.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Great. For the duplicate emails, you have two order notifications switched on, one in ShopStack and one in your email app. Turning one off fixes it. Shall I email you the steps?

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Yeah, send it. And the login?

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Your new hire's invitation expired after 72 hours. I've just sent a fresh one. Ask them to accept it today.

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Man, three for three. Can you circle back tomorrow and check the sync held?

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Sure. I'll check the sync logs and email you by 10 a.m. Central time tomorrow. Your case number is SS-41120.

lines.name: Jake Turner
lines.text: Appreciate it, Ravindu.

lines.name: Ravindu
lines.text: Anytime, Jake. Good luck with Black Friday.

scenarios.title: The fourth call about an estimated bill
scenarios.setting: Evening inbound call to Northway Energy, a UK gas and electricity supplier, handled by its customer team in Sri Lanka.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Chamari, 31, senior customer service agent. Customer: Linda Hughes, 58, from Cardiff, calling for the fourth time about a £612 estimated bill.
scenarios.resolution: The bill is corrected from £612 to £187 on the call, a formal complaint is logged, an engineer is booked with a named follow-up call, and everything is confirmed in writing by 7 p.m.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Agree with what is true (“That's not acceptable”) and accept doubt calmly (“That's fair”). Don't defend the colleagues who let her down.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: With a repeat caller, the only proof is action: the fix during the call, then three dated commitments (email by 7 p.m., engineer on Tuesday, a call at 1 p.m.).

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Reading the history and summarising it (“Have I got that right?”) means she doesn't have to repeat herself. That alone lowers the anger.

notes.label: call basics
notes.text: Log it as a formal complaint and tell the customer where she can go next (in UK energy, the Energy Ombudsman). Hiding the next step makes complaints worse.

sayThis.say: I'm going to correct the bill on this call

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: Good evening, Northway Energy. Calls are recorded. My name is Chamari. How can I help?

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: This is the fourth time I've called. The fourth! My bill says £612, and I have a smart meter. Nobody listens.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: I'm sorry you've had to call four times. That's not acceptable, and I can hear how fed up you are. Could I take your name and postcode, so I can read your history?

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: Linda Hughes, CF14 3AB. And I'm not explaining it all again.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: You won't need to. Thank you, Mrs Hughes. For security, could you confirm the last four digits of the bank account for your Direct Debit?

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: It ends 0917.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: Thank you. I've read the notes. Your smart meter stopped sending readings in July, so your bills since then have been estimated. You were told twice an engineer would come, and nobody did. Have I got that right?

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: Yes! And I've sent photos of the meter twice. What's the point?

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: The point is that your photos are here, and they show you've used far less than the estimate. I'm going to correct the bill on this call.

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: I'll believe it when I see it.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: That's fair. I'm entering the reading from your photo dated 20 October. Please bear with me for one minute while the bill recalculates.

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: Fine.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: Thank you for waiting. Your corrected bill is £187, not £612. I've also logged a formal complaint about the missed engineer visits, and booked an engineer for Tuesday the 3rd, between 8 a.m. and noon.

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: £187? So I've been worrying about £400 for nothing. And if they don't turn up again?

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: I'll call you at 1 p.m. on Tuesday to check. If they haven't come, I'll rebook it myself and arrange a goodwill credit for the missed visit.

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: Fine. But I want that in writing.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: You'll have an email by 7 p.m. tonight with the corrected bill, the engineer booking and your complaint reference, NE-30944. It also explains how to go to the Energy Ombudsman if you're still unhappy after eight weeks.

lines.name: Linda Hughes
lines.text: Right. Thank you, Chamari. You're the first one who's actually done something.

lines.name: Chamari
lines.text: Thank you for your patience, Mrs Hughes. I'll speak to you on Tuesday.

scenarios.title: Cancelled connection: “I want a supervisor”
scenarios.setting: Inbound call to Pacific Crest Airlines reservations, answered by its contact centre in Colombo. Evening in Dallas, after a crew-shortage cancellation.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Hiruni, 25, reservations agent. Supervisor: Roshan, 38, team leader, who joins at line 11. Customer: Mark Bennett, 44, travelling with his wife and two children.
scenarios.resolution: The family is rebooked together to Denver at 9:15 the next morning, with a hotel and meal vouchers that night. The supervisor joined through a warm handover, and the agent stays on the line until the vouchers arrive.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Respect the request for a supervisor without taking it personally. “I'll try first, and I'll bring my supervisor in myself” keeps control and the customer's trust.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: Even small waits get a limit: two minutes, a hold under a minute, vouchers within ten minutes.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: Hiruni's summary is so complete that Roshan can repeat it in one line. That is what a warm handover means: the customer never tells the story twice.

notes.label: escalation basics
notes.text: Escalate for a reason the customer can hear (“a partner airline needs supervisor approval”), not just “It's not my job.”

sayThis.say: Could I put you on a brief hold, under a minute?

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: Pacific Crest reservations, this is Hiruni. This call is recorded. How can I help?

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: My connection to Denver got cancelled. I'm in Dallas with my wife and two kids, and the app says the next flight is Saturday. That's two days!

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: I'm so sorry. That's a hard spot to be in with two children. May I have your confirmation code and last name?

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: K7QZ2M, Bennett. And I want a supervisor. I'm done with chatbots.

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: I understand, Mr. Bennett. You're speaking to a person, and I'll try first. If I can't fix it, I'll bring my supervisor on the line myself. Is that okay?

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: Fine. You've got two minutes.

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: Thank you. So: four passengers, Dallas to Denver, cancelled tonight, and Saturday isn't acceptable. Would you consider flying to Colorado Springs instead?

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: No. Our car's parked at Denver airport. I need Denver, tomorrow, all four of us together.

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: Understood. Our own flights tomorrow don't have four seats together. A partner airline needs supervisor approval, so I'll bring him in now. Could I put you on a brief hold, under a minute?

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: Okay. Under a minute.

lines.name: Roshan
lines.text: Mr. Bennett, this is Roshan, Hiruni's supervisor. She's told me everything: four of you, Denver, tomorrow, seats together. You don't need to repeat anything.

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: Finally. Can you get us out tomorrow?

lines.name: Roshan
lines.text: Yes. I've approved four seats on a partner flight at 9:15 tomorrow morning, together in row 22, at no extra charge.

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: Okay. That's more like it. What about tonight?

lines.name: Roshan
lines.text: Because the cancellation was caused by a crew shortage, we're covering a hotel near the airport and a $25 meal voucher for each of you. Hiruni will email them to you.

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: How fast?

lines.name: Hiruni
lines.text: Within ten minutes, Mr. Bennett, with the hotel shuttle details. I'll stay on the line until you confirm they've arrived.

lines.name: Mark Bennett
lines.text: Alright. Thank you both. Sorry I lost my temper.

lines.name: Roshan
lines.text: Please don't worry about it. It's been a long day. Have a safe flight tomorrow.

scenarios.title: The callback I missed
scenarios.setting: Outbound call from PayRight, a Colombo payroll provider, to a small-business client in Melbourne at 8:30 a.m. Melbourne time, the morning after a promised 3 p.m. callback didn't happen.
scenarios.characters: Agent: Malith, 33, payroll specialist. Client: Tom Nguyen, 47, owner of a plumbing business with 12 staff, including two apprentices.
scenarios.resolution: Malith calls before Tom has to chase him, owns the miss, fixes the underpayment with an off-cycle pay run, promises a super answer by 4 p.m., and adds a cut-off check so it doesn't happen again.

notes.label: empathy
notes.text: Name the cost of your mistake to the client (his staff ringing him all evening) and own it in one line: “That's on me.” No excuses about workload or time zones.

notes.label: timely response
notes.text: After a broken promise, make the next ones smaller and closer (11 a.m., 4 p.m.), and promise to warn the client before a time passes, not after.

notes.label: active listening
notes.text: “Is there anything else I've missed?” brings out the super question that would have caused a second complaint.
Call the client first: if you miss a callback, the recovery call should come from you, at the start of the client's day.

sayThis.say: I'll call you at 11 a.m. Melbourne time today
sayThis.not: I'll call you back today itself.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Hi Tom, it's Malith from PayRight in Colombo. I promised to call you by 3 p.m. yesterday, and I didn't. I'm sorry. That's on me.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Yeah, I noticed. My two apprentices were ringing me all evening asking where their overtime was.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: I can imagine how that put you in a tough spot with your team. I'd like to fix it properly now. Do you have ten minutes?

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Go on.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Thank you. For security, could you confirm the last three digits of your ABN?

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Yeah, 507.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Thanks. So last Thursday's pay run left out overtime for Jess and Liam, and they want to know when they'll be paid. Is there anything else I've missed?

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Liam reckons his super looked wrong too.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Thanks for telling me. The overtime was missed because the timesheets came in after the cut-off and weren't picked up. Jess is owed $412 and Liam $386, before tax.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: So when do they get it?

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: I'll prepare an off-cycle pay run today, and you'll have it to approve by 11 a.m. Melbourne time. Once you approve it, it usually reaches their accounts by the next business day.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: And Liam's super?

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Overtime usually doesn't attract super, but I'll check his ordinary hours line by line and email you the answer by 4 p.m. today.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Okay. How do I know you won't drop it again?

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Fair question. I've set two reminders, and my team leader, Anoma, is copied on this case. If I'm ever going to miss a time, I'll message you before it passes, not after.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Alright. And the late timesheets?

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: From next week, I'll check for late timesheets at the cut-off and message you if any are missing, so this doesn't happen again.

lines.name: Tom Nguyen
lines.text: Good. So: the pay run by 11, and the super answer by 4.

lines.name: Malith
lines.text: Exactly. I'll call you at 11 to walk you through the approval. Thanks for your patience, Tom.
